reference.source: NICE guideline on metastatic spinal cord compression
clinicalPearls: Progressive or unremitting back pain, often thoracic, band-like or worse on lying, coughing or straining, frequently precedes neurological signs by days to weeks and should trigger urgent whole-spine imaging.
The thoracic spine is the commonest site; multiple non-contiguous levels are present in up to a third of patients, so imaging must cover the entire spine, not just the symptomatic region.
Breast, lung, prostate, myeloma and renal malignancies account for most cases; MSCC is the presenting feature of cancer in a substantial minority.
Whole-spine MRI is the investigation of choice and should be obtained within 24 hours of suspicion (sooner if neurology is progressing).

Start high-dose corticosteroid (dexamethasone) with gastroprotection immediately on suspicion unless contraindicated—but withhold if untreated lymphoma is likely and tissue is needed, as steroids can lyse tumour and obscure diagnosis.
Ambulatory and continent status at presentation is the strongest predictor of functional outcome, underscoring the value of treating before deficits are established.

Definitive treatment is decompressive surgery (favoured for good performance status, single-level disease, spinal instability or radioresistant tumour) or radiotherapy; the choice depends on histology, prognosis and stability.
Nurse the patient flat with neutral spine alignment and log-roll until spinal stability is confirmed, and provide venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and bladder care.
reference.pathophysiology: Metastatic tumour, most often within a vertebral body, expands into the epidural space and compresses the thecal sac and cord (or cauda equina below the conus). Direct mechanical pressure is compounded by venous plexus obstruction causing vasogenic cord oedema, and by arterial compromise producing ischaemia and, ultimately, infarction. Vertebral collapse or retropulsed bone or tumour fragments may add an element of instability and further canal compromise. The progression from reversible oedema to irreversible infarction explains why outcome is time-critical and why neurological deficit, once fixed, seldom recovers.
additionalDifferentials: Benign disc prolapse or degenerative canal stenosis
Transverse myelitis or other inflammatory myelopathy
Pathological vertebral fracture without cord compression
additionalInvestigations: Urgent whole-spine MRI with and without contrast
CT of the spine to assess bony stability and for surgical planning
CT staging of chest, abdomen and pelvis to identify primary and disease extent
Prostate-specific antigen and myeloma screen where primary is unknown
Image-guided or surgical biopsy when the diagnosis of malignancy is not established
Bloods including calcium, renal and liver function
Bone scintigraphy or PET for disease mapping
redFlags: New or progressive limb weakness or gait disturbance
Bladder or bowel dysfunction (a late and ominous sign)
Severe, progressive or nocturnal thoracic spinal pain
Rapidly evolving neurological deficit over hours
reference.prognosis: Neurological outcome hinges on the deficit at the time treatment starts: patients ambulant at presentation usually remain so, whereas established paraplegia rarely reverses. Overall survival is governed by the underlying malignancy and its treatability rather than the compression itself.
pitfalls: Waiting for neurological signs before imaging in a cancer patient with new back pain
Imaging only the symptomatic level and missing higher or lower compressions
Giving corticosteroids before biopsy when lymphoma is the likely cause
Overlooking spinal instability and mobilising the patient prematurely
Attributing bladder dysfunction to opioids or immobility rather than to cord or cauda equina compromise
references: NICE clinical guideline on the diagnosis and management of metastatic spinal cord compression
DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
management: Treat as an oncologic emergency where preserving neurologic and sphincter function is the priority, not oncologic cure of the compression itself.

Obtain tissue diagnosis before treatment unless the patient already has known metastatic cancer; avoid starting steroids before biopsy when lymphoma is suspected, since steroids can obscure the histologic diagnosis.

Start corticosteroids (such as dexamethasone) promptly on clinical suspicion to reduce cord edema, without waiting for pathology once tissue is secured or cancer history is known; avoid very high trauma-protocol steroid regimens, which add complications without added benefit.

Assess performance status, prognosis, and available systemic therapy before choosing definitive local treatment; favor conservative or hospice-oriented care in poor-prognosis, widely metastatic patients, and active radiotherapy/surgery in those with better performance status and survival expectancy.
Apply a multidisciplinary framework assessing mechanical spinal stability, severity and duration of neurologic deficit, radiosensitivity of the tumor histology, and preferred treatment approach.
Refer for urgent surgical stabilization if the spine is mechanically unstable, regardless of radiosensitivity, rather than using radiotherapy alone up front.

Favor prompt surgical decompression for acute or short-duration deficits, since deficits complete for more than about three days are less likely to improve with surgery and are better managed with radiotherapy alone.

Consider surgical decompression followed by adjuvant radiotherapy for high-grade compression in surgical candidates, since surgery alone does not achieve durable control; weigh reduced benefit of surgery in elderly patients and avoid surgery when life expectancy is under about three months, using less invasive stabilizing procedures instead in poor surgical candidates.

Use separation surgery followed by stereotactic body radiotherapy for radioresistant tumors (such as renal cell carcinoma, sarcoma, or melanoma) to allow safe delivery of high-dose radiation near the cord.
Reserve stereotactic body radiotherapy as upfront treatment for low-grade compression only, since its high dose exceeds spinal cord tolerance in high-grade disease.

Consider systemic anticancer therapy (chemotherapy, targeted agents, or hormonal therapy) as primary or adjunct treatment for chemosensitive or hormone-sensitive histologies with low-grade, minimally symptomatic compression; note that radionuclide therapy is not effective for established epidural disease.

Provide supportive care in parallel with definitive treatment, including analgesia, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, bladder and bowel management, pressure-area care, gastroprotection with steroids, and spinal precautions until stability is confirmed.
Treat new back pain in a patient with known or suspected cancer as spinal metastasis with possible cord compression until proven otherwise, prompting urgent imaging and specialist referral.
Urgently involve spine surgery, radiation oncology, and medical oncology at diagnosis of high-grade compression or spinal instability, in parallel with steroid initiation and whole-spine imaging.
